analysis.one_liner: Requires testing and cleanup of lead paint hazards in federally assisted pre-1978 housing where young children live.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by nine senators from both parties, the bill never left the Senate Banking Committee, which held one hearing but took no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required owners of federally assisted housing built before 1978 to test for lead paint hazards when a family with a child under 6 moves in or renews a lease, then fix any hazards within 30 days and notify residents. If a landlord did not fix the hazard, the family could move to a safe unit immediately, with no waitlist, penalty, or gap in their housing assistance. It also authorized federal funding to carry out the new rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families with children under age 6 living in federally assisted housing built before 1978, the housing stock where lead paint hazards are most common. Young children are the ones most harmed by lead exposure, which can cause permanent developmental damage. Residents would also get written notice when hazards are found in their building.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young children in older assisted housing

how_it_helps.text: Owners of covered pre-1978 federally assisted housing must conduct a risk assessment for lead paint hazards — not just a visual check — within set deadlines when a family with a child under 6 will live in the unit, including within 15 days for units with Section 8 tenant-based vouchers.
If hazards are found, the owner must control them within 30 days, with no extensions, and must notify all affected residents and post notice in common areas.

If a family with a young child is living in a unit where hazards were found but not fixed, HUD must let them relocate immediately to a unit built in 1978 or later or to another hazard-free assisted unit, with no waitlist, no penalty, and no lapse in assistance.
The bill authorizes whatever appropriations are necessary to carry out the new requirements for fiscal years 2022 through 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of federally assisted pre-1978 housing, who would bear the cost of professional risk assessments and hazard control work, and federal taxpayers for any appropriated funds. Some of the landlord cost could ultimately reach renters through rents.

drawbacks.text: The 30-day deadline to control hazards, with no extension allowed under the bill, could be difficult and expensive for owners to meet, and some of that cost could be passed to tenants through higher rents or could push marginal units out of the assisted housing supply.
Requiring professional risk assessments rather than visual checks, and clearances after control work, adds recurring inspection costs for every covered unit where a young child moves in or renews.
The funding authorization is open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary'), so the full federal cost was not fixed in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is substantial: lead poisoning in young children causes lasting harm, and the bill targeted exactly the assisted housing stock where the risk concentrates, including an emergency relocation right so families are not trapped in a hazardous unit. The main costs are real but ordinary compliance costs for landlords and modest federal spending, and the bill included exceptions for owners who had recently tested and cleared their units. On balance a targeted, comparatively inexpensive safety rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which held one hearing on it but never voted to advance it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on May 26, 2021, joined by eight cosponsors split evenly between four Senate Democrats and four Senate Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The committee held a hearing on June 24, 2021, printing S.Hrg. 117-384, but took no further action on the bill.
No vote ever occurred in the Senate or the House, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords of federally assisted pre-1978 housing were better off because the bill died, since they never had to pay for required risk assessments and hazard cleanup; families with young children in that housing remained exposed to the risk the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at introduction — the bill was introduced by a Democrat with three Republicans among its cosponsors, for a total of four Democrats and four Republicans backing it — but no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of any final decision never got recorded.

industries.industry: Landlords of federally assisted pre-1978 housing
industries.note: The bill would have required these owners to pay for professional lead risk assessments when young children move in or renew, and to control any hazards within 30 days. Their cost is the safety benefit to child tenants, so their interest in blocking the bill ran against the families it would protect.

The bill's mandatory risk assessments, hazard control work, and clearance exams would have created steady new demand for certified lead inspectors and abatement contractors. Their interest ran alongside residents' safety.
